text.p: Hopewell Holdings Ltd's $3.2 billion Bangkok mass transit project appeared bogged down as unpaid contractors stopped work and talks with the Thai government reached an impasse, analysts said on Tuesday.

Thai officials have given Hopewell until end-July to come up with a firm project financing plan but Hopewell has shown no signs of meeting the government deadline, sources familiar with the project said.

Any meeting this week between Hopewell and Thai officials would be the first since Hopewell Chairman Gordon Wu said earlier this month the project's 40-km first phase may not be completed in time for the Bangkok Asian Games in December 1998.
The Thais have since threatened to cancel Wu's 30-year concession.
Construction of the elevated rail and road project, of which only about 17 percent of the first phase's civil and structural work is complete, has ground to a halt.
Contractors hired by Hopewell, unpaid for about three months, were pulling machinary and workers off the project, industry sources said.
Thai Bauer has the project's main piling job while other international and local constructors have contracts to build its elevated superstructure.
"All substantial work on the project has stopped at the moment," said an industry source.

"We've certainly reduced expediture to a minimum. With a flow of funds I dare say we could continue but we've made best use of our resources and minimised our exposure to Hopewell," said an executive of a contractor.
Some contractors have been given assurances that payment would be resumed in mid-August and a three month payment backlog cleared by end-September, they said.

The slow construction followed Hopewell's clashes with successive Thai governments over project terms for most of the past seven years. Contractors said the first phase is at least eight months behind schedule,
The situation is unlikely to be resolved by the two parties until Wu and his creditors see the troubled Thai economy recovering to a level making the project viable, analysts said.
"I think the company might try to hang on to the land rights waiting for the property market to turn around," said Philip Sheridan, property and land analyst at Thaimex Finance and Securities.
The property market is in a protracted slump affecting Hopewell's projected revenue to be earned from renting retail and commercial space related to the project.

Thailand's battered economy made Hopewell reluctant to commit financing to even a watered down contract, analysts said. But it also appeared Thailand's economic woes had put government negotiators in a weaker position, the sources said.

"Both parties have seen that it is very difficult for Hopewell to walk away and it is even more difficult for the Thai government to cancel the project," said Bob Kevorkian, Managing Director of K-Tech Construction and Engineering, one of the project's contractors.
